transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-15
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Tom Sinclair (Brightfield Head of ML), Sara Lee (Brightfield Platform Eng Lead), Marcus Huang (Brightfield CTO)

Auto-summary (auto): Quick discovery: evaluate Redwood's hosted API for a fast PoC vs a VPC/private pilot. Need to validate latency, cost, and security posture.

00:00 Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, uh this is Alex from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, and with me is Priya, our systems engineer. How are you all doing?
00:07 Tom: Good, thanks Alex. Tom here. Appreciate you setting this up. We've been talking in email, excited to understand the quickest path to a prototype.
00:12 Marcus: Hi, Marcus here. We'll mostly be listening but want to make sure the security and cost picture is clear.
00:18 Priya: Awesome. Quick agenda: 1) understand Brightfield's current stack and success criteria, 2) talk about our PLG quickstart (free credits, time-to-first-token), 3) hosted vs dedicated/VPC differences, and 4) next steps for a pilot and benchmarks. Sound OK?
00:28 Sara: Yep, that works. We have a little context: our stack is mostly Kubernetes on GCP, we have a private VPC, and we need SOC2-level controls for customer data. We also run real-time inference for document classification, so latency matters.
00:40 Alex: Great, that's helpful. Can you share baseline numbers -- what latency do you need at p95, and what QPS are we talking about for a pilot?
00:48 Tom: For the initial pilot it's low QPS, maybe 5-10 reqs/sec, but p95 latency ideally under 300ms for 512 token-ish responses. If we move to production we could see 100-200 reqs/sec.
00:58 Priya: Cool. Two things to call out: our hosted API is fastest to get running — we give credits and you can be issuing calls the same day; dedicated or private VPC gives isolation and brings in networking and onboarding steps so time-to-first-token goes up.
01:12 Marcus: What does 'goes up' look like? Days? Weeks?
01:15 Priya: Hosted: same day — set up org, allocate credits, test with SDK. Dedicated reserved capacity: typically a few days to provision if we have capacity; private VPC/on-prem: depends on network approvals and on prem packaging, usually 2-4 weeks. But we do fast-paths for pilots — we've done one-week VPC pilots when customers have pre-approved networking.
01:32 Tom: Ok. For security we need SOC2 report, audit logs, SSO (SAML), and the option for customer-managed keys if possible.
01:40 Alex: Yes, we can share SOC 2 Type II, our audit logs are available in the Console at the token/request level, SAML SSO is supported, and for Private deployments customer KMS/HSM can be integrated. For hosted, we use Redwood-managed keys but we offer strict data handling controls — though some customers require HSM, which pushes them to private.
01:56 Sara: If we start on hosted for speed, does that preclude later moving to VPC? How seamless is the migration?
02:03 Priya: Migration is designed to be seamless at the API level — same endpoints and SDKs, you can pin model versions and rollout policies. The main work is network setup and data residency policies, but from an app code standpoint it's minimal. We do recommend validating prompts and caching behavior during the migration.
02:19 Tom: Nice. On cost: are there big unit cost differences between hosted and dedicated?
02:24 Alex: Hosted is usage-based and typically slightly higher per-token than a committed dedicated pool — dedicated/reserved capacity buys lower unit cost at the expense of a commit. Private has similar economics to dedicated depending on your infra. Priya can run a quick estimate if you share workload characteristics.
02:37 Priya: Yes I can do that. If you share the prompt mix and sequence lengths I'll run a cost/latency matrix for hosted, reserved, and private. That will show per-token cost and expected p95 latency ranges.
02:49 Tom: We'll pull a sample prompt set after the call.
02:53 Marcus: About data retention — can you configure logs retention and redact inputs? We have to limit PII.
02:59 Priya: Hosted: you can control data retention in the Console and configure automatic redaction patterns. For private deployments you get full control over storage. Also we support per-route data policies and token-level masking in flight.
03:14 Alex: Quick question on PLG credits — the typical pattern is we provide trial credits tied to an account; you can use those to test the hosted API. The TTFT (time to first token) for a simple text completion is minutes after creating credentials — usually under 1 hour if you include onboarding steps.
03:29 Tom: Under one hour? That's what we want for the engineering sprint. Any gotchas for SDKs? We use a Python stack.
03:36 Priya: We have official SDKs for Python, Node, and Java. If you use our Python SDK it's pip install and a quick token env var. We'll send a quickstart repo link. There can be occasional transcribed name issues — for example the client lib uses the 'redwood' package, but we have wrapper examples for fast integration.
03:53 Sara: Ok. On private/VPC, what's required from our networking team? Firewall rules? VPN?
03:58 Priya: For a VPC peering or private link, we'll need CIDR ranges, approved ingress rules, and a static set of egress endpoints. If you go with a full private control plane we can swap to customer-managed VPN or Direct Connect equivalent. We provide a network checklist.
04:16 Tom: Does Redwood offer dedicated GPU pools for steady throughput? We've seen spiky loads with bursts when a backlog gets replayed.
04:22 Alex: Yes, our Dedicated product is premised on reserved GPU pools with autoscaling and burst capacity options. You can configure scaling policies and burst allowances. The runtime supports continuous batching and KV-cache management to reduce cost and keep latency predictable.
04:38 Marcus: Any references or case studies for similar customers in regulated sectors?
04:42 Alex: We can share anonymized case studies and a compliance pack. Priya, will you append the SOC2 and an example VPC network doc to the follow-up?
04:48 Priya: Yep, I'll include SOC2, network checklist, and a quick guide on private KMS integration.
04:53 Tom: Great. On latency benchmarking — can Redwood run a 1-day benchmark for hosted vs private so we can see p50/p95/P99?
04:59 Priya: Yes. We typically recommend a short benchmark: 1) run hosted with your prompt set using the trial credits, 2) run a dedicated/reserved config with same model and batch settings, and 3) if you want, run a VPC pilot. We can provision a dedicated pilot environment for a day and capture token-level traces. You'll get a spreadsheet with CPU/GPU utilization, per-route cost, and latency percentiles.
05:20 Sara: If we do that, what telemetry do you need from our side?
05:23 Priya: Sample prompt set, target concurrency/QPS, target latency SLOs, and any auth constraints (e.g. IP allowlist). If you have a synthetic load script that's great; otherwise we can generate load from our side against your test endpoints.
05:36 Tom: We'll send the prompts and a load profile.
05:39 Marcus: One more on keys — is there an option to bring your own key for hosted? We have strict KMS requirements and may need HSM-backed keys.
05:46 Alex: For hosted we don't support BYOK/HSM yet; that capability is in the Private installation path. Some enterprise customers use private control plane with KMS integration for HSM. We can map this into the pilot planning.
05:58 Tom: Noted. Another practical question: do you have pre-built integrations for observability? We have Datadog and internal tracing.
06:04 Priya: Yes, we emit traces and metrics and have a Datadog integration plus hooks for OpenTelemetry. In Dedicated or Private you can ship logs directly to your logging endpoint. For hosted we provide a secure export path.
06:15 Sara: Good. On-model catalog: do you host multiple open models and how do you recommend choosing one for our use case?
06:21 Alex: We curate a model catalog with performance profiles. For lower latency and cost you may choose a quantized variant; if you need higher quality then a larger variant is recommended. Priya can recommend model/quantization choices based on your prompt set.
06:33 Priya: Quick note — quantization and batch size have tradeoffs for latency and deterministic output. We'll show a matrix in the estimator I produce.
06:41 Tom: Cool. Any obvious blockers for a hosted-first pilot?
06:44 Alex: The main blocker would be if you require HSM/BYOK or strict on-prem data residency — that forces Private. Otherwise hosted gets you live fastest.
06:54 Marcus: And what about contract terms and minimums if we want dedicated later?
06:58 Alex: Dedicated is a reserved capacity contract — monthly/annual commits. For pilots we can provide short-term dedicated pilot capacity without a long-term commit to collect data. We'll include options in the pricing sheet.
07:10 Sara: Ok, let's capture the concrete next steps — can we recap?
07:14 Alex: Sure. Action items recap: Alex will send pilot pricing and T&Cs and allocate trial credits. Priya will send SOC2 report, VPC/network checklist, and run a cost/latency estimate once you send prompts. Tom will send the sample prompt set and QPS target. Sara will confirm any KMS/HSM requirements internally. We'll try to schedule the benchmark for week of 2026-05-25.
07:36 Tom: Sounds good. One little thing — sometimes the transcript examples I've seen refer to the 'KV cahce' — is that something you support? (laughs)
07:44 Priya: (laughs) We support KV cache for chat-like workloads; apologies for the transcribe misspelling there. It's spelled KV cache, and it helps keep token costs down for multi-turn conversations.
07:53 Marcus: Any final questions from Redwood side?
07:55 Alex: None here. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the docs and pricing.
07:59 Tom: Thanks Alex, Priya.
08:01 Sara: Thanks, bye.
